questions.html:
Consider the language $L$:

$L =$ {$ \langle \text{M} \rangle \mid \text{M}$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$, and there exists an input whose length is less than $100$, on which $\text{M}$ halts$\}$


Which of the following options is true?

options.html: $L$ is recursive.
$L$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive.
$L$ is not recursively enumerable.
$L$ is regular.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

"$\text{containing at least one string of length less than 100}$" is a non-trivial, but monotonous property for RE languages, hence by Rice Theorem, $L$ is undecidable.

$L$ is RE because for any member $M$ of $L$, we run $M$ on all strings of length at most $100$ in an interleaved mode (dovetailing), and we halt if $M$ accepts at least one such string. (Note that since we are running a member $M$ of $L$, so, $M$ is guaranteed to halt on at least one such string)

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Option : B

questions.html:
Consider the language $L$ defined as follows.
$$L = \left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
\{0\} & \text{if God does not exist} \\\\
\{1\} & \text{if God exists}
\end{array}
\right.$$
Which of the following option is correct ?

(Note that the answer does not depend on your religious convictions.)

options.html: $L$ is recursive
$L$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive
$L$ is not recursively enumerable
Whether $L$ is recursively enumerable or not will be known after we find out if God exists or not.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Note that whatever happens, whether God exists or not, $L$ contains only a single string, so $L$ is a finite language, hence, regular, hence decidable.

$L$ is recursive. $L = \{0\}$ or $L = \{1\}$, and for each possibility there is a TM that decides it!

Similar PYQ: https://gateoverflow.in/904/gate-cse-2003-question-13

options.html: Every turing machine recognizable language is recursive.
The complement of a recursive language is recursively enumerable.
The complement of a context-free language is context-free.
The set of turing machines which do not halt on empty input forms a recursively enumerable set

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

  1. FALSE. Halting Problem is turing machine recognizable but it is not recursive.
     
  2. TRUE. Recursive langauges are closed under complementation. So, complement of recursive language is recursive and therefore recursively enumerable because every recursive language is RE.
     
  3. FALSE. Complement of contex free langauge may or may not be context free. Counter example: $L = \{ a^nb^nc^n \mid n \ge0 \}$.
    $L'$ is context free but its complement $L'' = L$ is not context free.
     
  4. FALSE. It forms non recursively enumerable set
    i.e. $L = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid \text{M is TM and it does not halt on } \epsilon\}$ is not recursively enumerable.

questions.html: If $L$ is a decidable language, then which of the following is/are TRUE ?

options.html: $L$ is recognizable
$L'$ is recognizable
$L'$ is decidable
There is a Turing machine that halts on all inputs, accepting every string in $L$

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Decidable langauges are closed under complementation. And every decidable langauage is recursively enumerable.

So, if $L$ is decidable language then

  • $L$ is recognizable
  • $L'$ is decidable
  • $L'$ is also decidable
Option $D$ is also true because it is definiton of decidable langauge.
 
Correct options: $A,B,C,D$

questions.html: Which of the following problems is undecidable?

options.html: Membership Problem for TMs
Emptiness Problem for FSAs
Equivalence Problem for FSAs
Finiteness Problem for CFGs

questions.solution:
Answer: A

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

Membership Problem for TMs is undecidable.

Emptiness Problem for FSAs is decidable.
For a finite automaton, we can check whether any accepting state is reachable from the start state.
If reachable, then language is non-empty, otherwise empty. Hence decidable.

Equivalence Problem for FSAs is decidable. 
Given two FSAs, we can construct their symmetric difference automaton and test emptiness.

Finiteness Problem for CFGs is decidable.
Remove useless symbols from given CFG, then check if there exists a cycle A ⇒⁺ αAβ in variables. If such cycle exists then infinite language; otherwise finite.

Correct Answer: $A$

options.html: A non-deterministic TM can decide languages that a deterministic TM cannot decide.
If a language $L$ is context-free then $L'$ is TM decidable.
The Language $L = \{\langle M,w \rangle \mid M$ is a $ \text{Turing Machine}$ and $ w \notin L(M)\}$ is TM recognizable.
The language $L = \{\langle D \rangle \mid D$ is $\text{DFA}$ and $ L(D) $ is $\text{regular}\}$ is decidable.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

A. A non-deterministic TM can decide languages that a deterministic TM cannot decide.
FALSE. $\textbf{Non-Deterministic TM}$ is equivalent to $\textbf{Deterministic TM}$.

B. If a language $L$ is context-free then $L'$ is TM decidable.
TRUE. If $L$ is context free, then $L$ is also decidable. Decidable languages are closed under complementation. So, $L'$ is also decidable.

C. The Language $L = \{\langle M,w \rangle \mid M$ is a $ \text{Turing Machine}$ and $ w \notin L(M)\}$ is TM recognizable.
FALSE. $L$ is not TM recognizable.
$L$ is complement of $A_{TM}$ (Acceptance Problem for TMs). $A_{TM}$ is recursive but not RE. Complement of $\text{REC but not RE}$ langauge is always non-RE.

D. The language $L = \{\langle D \rangle \mid D$ is $\text{DFA}$ and $ L(D) $ is $\text{regular}\}$ is decidable.
TRUE. $L$ is trivially decidable because language of any $\text{DFA}$ is always regular!

questions.html:
Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ be the following languages:

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$, $N$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$ that halts on all inputs, and $N \in L(M)\}$

$L_2 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$, $N$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$ that halts on all inputs, and $M \in L(N)\}$

Which of the following options is correct?

options.html: Only $L_1$ is decidable
Only $L_2$ is decidable
Both $L_1$ and $L_2$ are decidable
Neither $L_1$ nor $L_2$ is decidable

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$, $N$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$ that halts on all inputs, and $N \in L(M)\}$

Here, $N$ is fixed TM and input is Turing Machine $M$.
According to Rice Theorem, "$N \in L(M)$" is non trivial property for recursively enumerable languages. So, $L_1$ is undecidable.

$L_2 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$, $N$ is a $\text{Turing Machine}$ that halts on all inputs, and $M \in L(N)\}$

Here also, $N$ is fixed TM and input is Turing Machine $M$. But question is, given Turing Machine $M$, does it belong to $L(N)?$
For a decider, we can always determine if any string is accepted by it or not. So, $L_2$ is decidable.

Correct Answer: $B$

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Thanks

options.html: The language $L = \{\langle \text{M}\rangle \ \mid \ \text{M}$ is a Turing machine and $L(M)$ is regular$\}$ is undecidable.
If $L_1, L_2$ are two decidable languages, and $L$ is a language such that $L_1 \subseteq L \subseteq L_2$, then $L$ is decidable.
If a language $L$ is recursively enumerable and its complement $L'$ is recursively enumerable, then $L$ is decidable.
There are undecidable languages over the alphabet containing only one symbol.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 0)

A: According to rice theorem, being regular is non-trivial (and also non-monotonic) property for recursively enumerable languages. So, $L$ is undecidable (and also not recursively enumerable).


B: Take $L_1 = \text{Empty Language}$, $L_2 = \text{Sigma}^*$. Now take any undecidable language as $L$.


C: $L$ & $L'$ are RE if and only if $L$ is Recursive.

Watch this!   

If a language $L$ and its complement $L'$ are both recursively enumerable, then both languages are recursive. If $L$ is recursive, then $L'$ is also recursive, and consequently both are recursively enumerable.

If a language and its complement are both RE then both are recursive.

A language is recursive if and only if both it and its complement are r.e.


D: There exists an undecidable unary language, since the number of unary languages is uncountable whereas the number of decidable languages is countably infinite!

questions.html:
Which of the following is/are decidable?

$L_1 = \{\langle M \rangle \mid M$ is a $ \text{DFA}$ that doesnt accept any string containing an odd number of $\text{1s}\} $

$L_2 = \{\langle G \rangle \mid G$ is a $ \text{CFG}$ over $\{1\}$ and $1^* \subseteq L(G)\}$

options.html: Only $L_1$
Only $L_2$
Both $L_1$ and $L_2$
Neither $L_1$ nor $L_2$

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

For $L_1$: Over regular languages or FAs, almost everything is decidable, No direct counter example exists on the internet which only uses FAs and is undecidable.

All decision problems about regular languages (given only DFA/NFA/RE, Not involving TM/PDA etc) are decidable.

$L_1$ can be written as $L_1 = \{ \langle \text{M} \rangle \mid \text{M is DFA and } L(M) \cap  L_{odd} = \phi\}$ where $L_{odd}$ is set of strings containing odd number of 1s.

For a given $\text{DFA M}$, both $L(M)$ and $L_{odd}$ are regular. And disjointness problem of regular languages is decidable. Therefore we have algorithm to check if $L(M) \cap  L_{odd}$ is empty or not. So, $L_1$ is decidable.

For $L_2$: First watch this.   

Each unary context-free language is regular.
$$1^* \subseteq L(G) \Longleftrightarrow L(G) \cap 1^* = 1^*$$
Now define:
$$L' = L(G) \cap 1^*$$

  • CFL $\cap$ Regular $\Rightarrow$ CFL
     
  • So $L'$ is a CFL over unary alphabet $\{1\}$

Now the problem reduces to: Does a unary CFL equal $1^*$ ?

This is decidable because: Unary CFLs are always regular.

So, $L'$ is regular. Now checking $L' = 1^*$ or not, is decidable.

Official discussion page

questions.html:
Suppose there are four languages $A$, $B$, $C$, and $D$. Each of the languages may or may not be recursively enumerable. However, we know the following about them:

  • There is a mapping reduction (i.e., an algorithm which can be carried out by some Turing machine, not necessarily polynomial-time) from $\text{A}$ to $\text{B}.$ 
  • There is a mapping reduction from $\mathrm{B}$ to $\mathrm{C}$.
  • There is a mapping reduction from $\mathrm{D}$ to $\mathrm{C}$


Which of the following options is/are TRUE?

options.html: If $C$ is recursively enumerable, then $A$ is recursively enumerable.
If the complement of $B$ is not recursive, then the complement of $A$ is not recursive.
If $C$ is recursive, then the complement of $D$ is recursively enumerable.
If $C$ is recursively enumerable, then $B \cap D$ is recursively enumerable.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Learn about Mapping Reduction in crystal clear way:

Reductions - Part 1   

Reductions - Part 2   

Let $L_1$ and $L_2$ are two languages.

If there is mapping reduction from $L_1$ to $L_2$ then following statements are true:

  • If $L_2$ is decidable then $L_1$ is decidable.
  • If $L_1$ is undecidable then $L_2$ is also undecidable. (Contrapositive of above)
  • If $L_2$ is recursively enumerable then $L_1$ is recursively enumerable.
  • If $L_1$ is not recursively enumerable then $L_2$ is also not recursively enumerable. (Contrapositive of above)
In other words, we can say that undecidability flows in forward direction and decidability flows in backward direction.
 
Now, according to question:

A. If $C$ is recursively enumerable, then $A$ is recursively enumerable.
TRUE. If $C$ is recursively enumerable, then $B$ is recursively enumerable. And If $B$ is recursively enumerable, then $A$ is recursively enumerable. So, by transitivity, option $A$ is correct.

B. If the complement of $B$ is not recursive, then the complement of $A$ is not recursive.
Take the contrapositive:
If the complement of $A$ is recursive, then the complement of $B$ is recursive.
In other words, question is asking if $A$ is recursive, then $B$ is recursive.
FALSE.

C. If $C$ is recursive, then the complement of $D$ is recursively enumerable.
TRUE. If $C$ is recursive, then $D$ is also recursive and therefore recursively enumerable.

D. If $C$ is recursively enumerable, then $B \cap D$ is recursively enumerable.
TRUE. If $C$ is RE then $B$ and $D$ are also RE. We know that RE languages are closed under intersection. Therefore, $B \cap D$ is recursively enumerable.

Correct Answer: $\text{ACD}$
